prompt: A car in the lane next to you has stopped at a crosswalk, but you cannot see why. What should you do?
choices: Pass it slowly with your horn ready
Slow down and stop too; do not pass the stopped car
Change lanes away from it and keep going
Pass it if the crosswalk light is not flashing
explanation: A vehicle stopped at a crosswalk may be waiting for a pedestrian you cannot see. Never pass a vehicle that is stopped for pedestrians.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, NY p. 68, NJ p. 146)

prompt: A pedestrian using a white cane or a guide dog is waiting to cross in front of you. What should you do?
choices: Tap your horn so the person knows where you are
Go first if the person has not yet stepped off the curb
Yield only if the person is in a marked crosswalk
Yield the right-of-way and let the person cross
explanation: A white cane or guide dog usually means the person is blind or has low vision. Always yield to them, and do not use your horn, which can confuse or startle them.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 48, PA p. 59, NY p. 68)

prompt: Your light is red and you roll to a stop. Why should you NOT stop with your car in the middle of the crosswalk?
choices: It is only a problem if the crosswalk is painted yellow
Your car could be scratched by shopping carts
Pedestrians, including blind pedestrians, may be forced to walk around your car into traffic
Cross traffic will not be able to see your brake lights
explanation: Stopping in a crosswalk blocks the path pedestrians expect to use and can force them, especially blind pedestrians, out into moving traffic. Stop before the crosswalk.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 48, NJ p. 146, NY p. 68)

prompt: A pedestrian starts to cross at an intersection that has no painted crosswalk lines. What should you do?
choices: Keep going, because pedestrians must use a marked crosswalk
Yield to the pedestrian, because intersections can have unmarked crosswalks
Honk to warn the pedestrian to wait
Yield only if there is a traffic signal at the corner
explanation: Pedestrians have the right-of-way in marked and unmarked crosswalks. A crosswalk can exist at an intersection even when no lines are painted.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, NJ p. 146, NY p. 68)

prompt: A pedestrian stepped off the curb on a WALK signal. Halfway across, the signal changes and your light turns green. What should you do?
choices: Go, because the pedestrian no longer has the right-of-way
Drive slowly around the pedestrian
Wait until the pedestrian has finished crossing
Honk to hurry the pedestrian along
explanation: A pedestrian who has already started crossing must be allowed to finish, even if the signal changes while they are in the street.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 29, NJ p. 146)

prompt: You have a green light and are turning right. A pedestrian is crossing the street you are turning into. What should you do?
choices: Turn quickly before the pedestrian reaches your lane
Stop and let the pedestrian finish crossing before you turn
Turn, because a green light gives you the right-of-way
Sound your horn and turn slowly
explanation: When turning, you must yield to pedestrians in the crosswalk you are crossing. Many pedestrian crashes happen during turns when drivers watch only for other cars.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 68, NJ p. 147, PA p. 59)

prompt: An older pedestrian is still crossing slowly when your light turns green. What should you do?
choices: Drive forward slowly to show you are waiting
Go if the person is no longer in your lane
Tap your horn to let the person know the light changed
Wait patiently until the person reaches the other side
explanation: Older people, people with disabilities and adults with small children may need extra time to cross. Give them the time they need.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, PA p. 59)

prompt: You are stopped in the right lane of a four-lane road for a pedestrian waiting at the curb. Why should you NOT wave the person across?
choices: Drivers in the other lanes may not see the pedestrian and may not stop
Waving is only allowed at marked crosswalks
The pedestrian must wait for a WALK signal at every crossing
It makes the drivers behind you think you are turning
explanation: Your car can hide the pedestrian from drivers in the other lanes. It is never safe to wave a pedestrian into the path of traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 59, NJ p. 147)

prompt: Before you back out of a driveway in a neighborhood with children, what should you do?
choices: Rely on your rear-view mirror
Back out quickly so you spend less time in the street
Honk once and then back out
Check carefully behind your vehicle for small children before and while backing
explanation: Small children can be hidden behind a vehicle. Look carefully behind you before and while you back up.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 68, PA p. 59)

prompt: Why should you take extra care when children are playing near the street?
choices: Children always cross only at corners
Children have the right-of-way only on school days
Children may run into the street without looking
Children can easily judge how fast cars are moving
explanation: Children do not always understand danger and may dart out from between parked cars. Slow down and be ready to stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 59, NJ p. 147, NY p. 68)

prompt: A pedestrian is crossing in the middle of the block, not at a crosswalk, in front of you. What should you do?
choices: Keep going, because the pedestrian is breaking the law
Honk and keep your speed so the pedestrian moves
Slow down or stop to avoid hitting the pedestrian
Steer around the pedestrian without slowing
explanation: Even when a pedestrian is crossing where they should not, drivers must use caution, slow down or stop to let them finish crossing safely.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 47, NJ p. 147)

prompt: When riding on the road, bicyclists have:
choices: Fewer rights than drivers, because bicycles are slower
The right to ignore traffic signals
The same rights and responsibilities as other drivers
Rights only when they are in a bike lane
explanation: Bicyclists share the road and must follow the same traffic laws. Drivers must yield to them just as they would to another vehicle.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 52, NY p. 69, AZ p. 50)

prompt: You have parked on a busy street. What should you do before opening your door on the traffic side?
choices: Open the door a little so others know you are getting out
Turn on your hazard lights and open the door
Nothing, because traffic must go around open doors
Check your mirror and look over your shoulder for bicyclists and other traffic
explanation: Opening a door into the path of a bicyclist can cause a serious crash. Look for bicyclists approaching from behind before you open the door.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 69, FL p. 89, NJ p. 153)

prompt: You are about to turn right, and a bicyclist is riding in the bike lane next to you. What should you do?
choices: Speed up and turn in front of the bicyclist
Turn, because cars have the right-of-way over bicycles
Honk so the bicyclist stops for you
Yield to the bicyclist and make your turn behind them
explanation: When your turn crosses a bike lane, you must yield to bicyclists in it. Let them pass and then turn behind them.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., FL p. 89, NJ p. 153, CA p. 54)

prompt: In which direction must bicyclists ride on the road?
choices: Against traffic, so they can see oncoming cars
In the same direction as traffic
In either direction they choose
Against traffic on two-lane roads only
explanation: Bicyclists ride with the flow of traffic, so drivers should expect them on the right side of their own lane or road.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 53, NY p. 69, AZ p. 50)

prompt: A bicyclist ahead of you suddenly moves left, away from the edge of the road, to get around a pothole. What does this mean for you?
choices: The bicyclist is breaking the law by leaving the edge
The bicyclist is signaling you to pass on the right
The bicyclist is about to stop
This is allowed, so be ready for bicyclists to move left to avoid hazards
explanation: Bicyclists may legally move away from the right edge to avoid hazards such as potholes, debris or parked cars, and to prepare for a left turn. Give them room.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 52, AZ p. 50, FL p. 89)

prompt: Why should you slow down when you pass a bicyclist?
choices: Bicyclists are required to stop when they are passed
Your tires could throw water on the bicyclist
The rush of air from a fast-moving vehicle can push a bicyclist off balance
Passing slowly lets the bicyclist read your license plate
explanation: Air pressure from a vehicle passing quickly can make a bicyclist wobble or fall. Reduce speed and give plenty of room when passing.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 68, NY p. 70, PA p. 60)

prompt: You are coming up behind a bicyclist. Should you honk to let them know you are passing?
choices: Yes, you must always honk before passing a bicyclist
No, a loud horn can startle the bicyclist and cause a crash
Yes, but only on roads without a bike lane
No, because bicyclists must look behind them every few seconds
explanation: Avoid honking close to bicyclists unless it is needed to prevent a crash. A sudden horn can startle a rider into swerving or falling.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 50, PA p. 60, FL p. 89)

prompt: You just passed a bicyclist and want to turn right at the next driveway a short distance ahead. What is the safest choice?
choices: Slow down, let the bicyclist go by, and turn right behind them
Speed up so you can turn before the bicyclist reaches the driveway
Turn immediately after passing, since you are already ahead
Stop in the bike lane and wait for the bicyclist to go around you
explanation: Turning or braking right in front of a bicyclist you just passed can cut them off. Do not slow or stop suddenly in front of them; let them pass first and turn behind.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 60, FL p. 89, NJ p. 153)

prompt: You are waiting to turn left at an intersection. A bicyclist is coming straight toward you from the other direction. What should you do?
choices: Yield to the bicyclist, as you would to an oncoming car
Turn first, because bicycles must yield to cars
Turn quickly, because bicycles are slow
Flash your lights to tell the bicyclist to stop
explanation: When turning left, yield to all oncoming traffic, including bicyclists. Do not underestimate how fast a bicycle is moving.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 153, NY p. 69, FL p. 89)

prompt: You are behind a bicyclist on a narrow two-lane road with oncoming traffic and no room to pass safely. What should you do?
choices: Pass while staying in your lane, as close to the center line as you can
Honk until the bicyclist rides onto the shoulder
Follow closely so you are ready to pass the moment there is a gap
Slow down, follow at a safe distance, and pass only when it is safe
explanation: If you cannot give a bicyclist enough room, do not squeeze past. Stay back and wait until oncoming traffic clears and you can pass safely.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 54, MT p. 53, FL p. 89)

prompt: How much of a traffic lane is a motorcycle entitled to use?
choices: Half of the lane
The full width of the lane, the same as a car
Only the right part of the lane
Only as much as it needs, so a car may share the lane
explanation: A motorcycle is entitled to a full lane and may need the room to maneuver. Never try to share a lane with a motorcycle.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 58, PA p. 60, AZ p. 51)

prompt: What is the most common type of crash between a car and a motorcycle?
choices: A car turning left in front of an oncoming motorcycle
A motorcycle rear-ending a car
A car backing into a parked motorcycle
A motorcycle hitting a car head-on on a curve
explanation: Many car-motorcycle crashes happen at intersections when a driver turns left across the path of a motorcycle they did not see or misjudged.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 58, PA p. 60, AZ p. 50)

prompt: Why is it hard to judge the speed and distance of an approaching motorcycle?
choices: Its small size makes it seem farther away and slower than it really is
Motorcycles always travel faster than the speed limit
Motorcycle headlights are brighter than car headlights
Motorcycles do not have taillights
explanation: Because a motorcycle is small, it can appear farther away and slower than it actually is. Take a second look and allow extra time.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 71, AZ p. 51, TX p. 58)

prompt: A motorcycle approaching an intersection has its right turn signal flashing. You want to pull out in front of it. What should you do?
choices: Pull out, because the rider has signaled a turn
Pull out if the rider has slowed down a little
Wait until you are sure the motorcycle is actually turning
Flash your lights and then pull out
explanation: Motorcycle turn signals often do not cancel by themselves, and riders may forget to turn them off. Do not pull out until you see the motorcycle turning.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 58, PA p. 60, AZ p. 51)

prompt: Why might a motorcyclist suddenly change speed or position within the lane?
choices: To invite you to share the lane
To show that they are about to turn
Because riders must change position every few seconds by law
To avoid hazards such as gravel, potholes, grates or debris
explanation: Road conditions that are minor to a car can be dangerous for a motorcycle. Expect riders to adjust speed or lane position, and give them room.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 58, NJ p. 148, AZ p. 51)

prompt: Why do drivers often fail to see motorcycles?
choices: Motorcycles are not allowed to use headlights
Motorcycles usually ride on the shoulder
Motorcycles are only on the road in summer
Drivers tend to look for cars, and motorcycles are small and easy to miss
explanation: Many drivers look only for cars and trucks. A motorcycle's small size lets it blend in or hide in blind spots, so look for them on purpose.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 58, NY p. 72, NJ p. 149)

prompt: Before changing lanes on a busy highway, why should you make a special check for motorcycles?
choices: Motorcycles must always stay in the left lane
Motorcycles are small and can easily be hidden in your blind spot
Motorcycles are louder than cars, so you will hear them
Motorcycles cannot change lanes
explanation: A motorcycle can disappear in a blind spot or be missed in a quick look. Check your mirrors and turn your head before changing lanes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 58, CA p. 50, NJ p. 148)

prompt: It is raining and dark, and you are following a motorcycle. What should you do?
choices: Follow closer so your headlights help the rider see
Leave even more space than you normally would behind a motorcycle
Keep the same space you use in dry daylight
Pass the motorcycle as soon as possible
explanation: Rain and darkness make it harder for riders to stop and for you to see them. Give motorcycles even more following distance in these conditions.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 73, PA p. 60)

prompt: A motorcycle is passing you on the left. What should you do?
choices: Keep your speed and lane position so the rider can complete the pass
Move toward the left side of your lane
Speed up so the rider passes faster
Brake hard to let the rider in
explanation: When a motorcycle passes you, hold your speed and position and give the rider room to finish the pass and return to their lane.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 149)

prompt: A motorcycle is riding on the left side of the lane ahead of you, leaving open space on the right. May you drive into that space beside it?
choices: No, the motorcycle is entitled to the whole lane
Yes, if the space is at least as wide as your car
Yes, if you stay under the speed limit
Yes, if you signal first
explanation: Even when there seems to be room, do not share a lane with a motorcycle. The rider is entitled to the full lane and may need it to maneuver.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 58, AZ p. 51, CA p. 50)

prompt: At night you are waiting to turn left and see a single headlight coming toward you. What is the safest way to think about it?
choices: It is probably a car with a broken headlight, so it is safe to turn
A single light means the vehicle is far away
It is a bicycle, so you have plenty of time
It may be a motorcycle that is closer and faster than it looks, so wait unless you are sure
explanation: A single headlight gives fewer clues for judging distance and speed. It could be a motorcycle, so do not turn unless you are sure you have enough time.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 51, TX p. 58)

prompt: What are the No-Zones around a large truck or bus?
choices: Blind spots where the driver cannot see other vehicles
Areas where trucks are not allowed to drive
Lanes where cars may not pass trucks
Places where trucks may not park
explanation: No-Zones are large blind spots in front of, behind and beside a truck or bus. A car in a No-Zone can disappear from the driver's view.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 48, PA p. 60, NJ p. 149)

prompt: You are behind a large truck and cannot see the truck's side mirrors. What does this mean?
choices: You are at a safe following distance
The truck driver can see you in the rear camera
The truck is about to turn
The truck driver cannot see you
explanation: If you cannot see the truck's mirrors or the driver's face in them, the driver cannot see you. Drop back or move to where you are visible.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 48, TX p. 57, PA p. 61)

prompt: A large truck ahead is signaling a right turn but swings to the left, leaving a gap between it and the curb. What should you do?
choices: Stay behind the truck and do not try to pass on the right
Drive into the gap and pass on the right
Pass on the left because the truck is in the left lane
Honk so the driver knows you are there
explanation: Large trucks often swing left to make a right turn. A car that squeezes between the truck and the curb can be crushed. Stay back until the turn is complete.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 57, AZ p. 52, FL p. 92)

prompt: You have passed a large truck. When is it safe to move back into the truck's lane?
choices: When you can see the whole front of the truck in your rear-view mirror
As soon as your rear bumper is past the truck's front bumper
When the truck driver honks
As soon as you have signaled
explanation: Do not cut back in until you can see the entire front of the truck in your rear-view mirror. Then keep your speed; do not slow down in front of it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 57, NY p. 74, NJ p. 151)

prompt: Compared with a car going the same speed, a loaded tractor-trailer usually:
choices: Needs a much longer distance to stop
Stops in a shorter distance because it has more brakes
Stops in about the same distance
Stops faster on wet roads because it is heavier
explanation: Heavy trucks take much longer to stop than cars, and the heavier and faster the truck, the longer it takes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 48, TX p. 57, NY p. 74)

prompt: On which side should you pass a large truck?
choices: The right side, because trucks drive on the left
Either side, whichever is faster
The right side, but only on a highway
The left side, where the driver can see you better
explanation: Pass trucks on the left. The No-Zone on a truck's right side is especially large and dangerous, so the driver may not see a car passing there.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 49, FL p. 92, NJ p. 151, GA p. 9)

prompt: What is the safest way to pass a large truck on a highway?
choices: Pass steadily and without delay, so you do not stay beside the truck
Slow down beside the truck so the driver can see you
Stay beside the truck until the driver waves you on
Pass on the right, where the lane is usually clear
explanation: The sides of a truck are No-Zones. Complete your pass without lingering alongside, then move back only when it is safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 60, NJ p. 152, CA p. 49)

prompt: You stop behind a truck at a traffic light on an uphill street. What should you do?
choices: Pull up close so cars behind you have more room
Leave extra space in front of you, because the truck may roll back when it starts
Stop beside the truck instead
Turn on your high beams so the driver sees you
explanation: Trucks and buses can roll backward slightly when starting on a hill. Leaving space also lets you pull around if needed.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 75, TX p. 57, PA p. 61, NJ p. 151)

prompt: You are following a large truck at night. What should you do with your headlights?
choices: Use high beams so the driver knows you are there
Flash your high beams every few seconds
Turn on your fog lights and high beams together
Use low beams, because high beams reflect off the truck's mirrors into the driver's eyes
explanation: Bright lights from behind reflect off a truck's large side mirrors and can blind the driver. Dim your headlights when following.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 57, PA p. 61, FL p. 91)

prompt: A large truck is coming toward you on a two-lane road. What should you do?
choices: Move toward the center line to avoid the shoulder
Speed up to get past it quickly
Keep as far to the right in your lane as is safe
Flash your high beams to warn the driver
explanation: Keeping to the right reduces the chance of a sideswipe and lessens the wind blast between your car and the truck.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 57, NJ p. 152, NY p. 75)

prompt: When you meet a large truck coming from the opposite direction, what does the wind turbulence between the two vehicles do?
choices: It pulls the vehicles together
It has no effect on a car
It pushes the vehicles apart
It pushes both vehicles toward the shoulder
explanation: The air blast from a passing truck pushes vehicles apart, not together. Keep both hands on the wheel and stay to the right of your lane.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 57, PA p. 61)

prompt: A large truck is passing you on a highway. How can you help?
choices: Speed up so the truck finishes passing quickly
Move toward the truck so it has a shorter distance to pass
Brake hard so the truck can pull in sooner
Keep to the far side of your lane and do not speed up
explanation: When a truck passes you, stay on the far side of your lane and hold or slightly reduce your speed. Never speed up while being passed.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 57, PA p. 61, FL p. 92)

prompt: You want to pass a large truck just as the road begins a long downhill grade. What should you expect?
choices: The truck will slow down, making it easier to pass
The truck must move to the shoulder to let you by
The truck may pick up speed, so the pass could take much longer
The truck's speed will not change
explanation: A heavy truck often slows going uphill but gains speed going downhill. Passing on a downgrade can leave you beside the truck much longer than you planned.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 57, NY p. 75, FL p. 92)

prompt: A truck is blocking the road while it backs into a loading dock. What should you do?
choices: Drive quickly behind the truck before it reaches you
Honk so the driver stops backing
Wait until the truck finishes backing; never pass close behind it
Pass behind the truck if you have room
explanation: The area behind a truck is a large blind spot. A car that passes behind a backing truck may not be seen. Be patient and wait.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 57, NY p. 75, PA p. 62)

prompt: Why can a large truck reach an intersection sooner than you expect?
choices: Trucks are allowed to drive faster than cars
Its large size makes it look like it is moving slower than it really is
Trucks have the right-of-way at intersections
Trucks speed up when approaching intersections
explanation: Because of its size, a truck often appears to move slower than it is. Do not underestimate its speed when turning or crossing in front of it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 58, NY p. 75, CA p. 49)

prompt: You need to take the next exit, but a large truck is in the right lane just ahead of the exit. What is the safest choice?
choices: Speed up and cut in front of the truck to reach the exit
Pass the truck on the right shoulder
Slow down and exit behind the truck
Stop in your lane until the truck moves
explanation: Never cut in front of a truck to reach an exit. Taking a few extra seconds to slow down and exit behind it keeps the truck's stopping space clear.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 74, TX p. 57, CA p. 49)

prompt: You are about to turn across light rail or streetcar tracks, and a train is approaching. What should you do?
choices: Turn quickly before it arrives
Wait for the train to pass; never turn in front of it
Turn if the train sounds its horn
Stop on the tracks until the driver waves you on
explanation: Light rail vehicles cannot stop quickly or steer around you. Check for them before turning across the tracks and never turn in front of one.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 50, TX p. 59)

prompt: A school bus ahead turns on its flashing yellow lights. What does this mean?
choices: The bus is stopped and you must stop now
The bus has finished loading and you may pass
You must pass the bus quickly before it stops
The bus is getting ready to stop, so slow down and prepare to stop
explanation: Flashing yellow (amber) lights warn that the bus is about to stop to load or unload children. Slow down and be ready to stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 56, NY p. 40, PA p. 62)

prompt: You are behind a school bus that stops with red lights flashing and its stop arm out. What must you do?
choices: Stop and stay stopped until the red lights stop flashing
Pass slowly on the left
Stop, then go when you think the children are safe
Pass if no children are in sight
explanation: When a school bus shows flashing red lights and its stop arm, traffic behind it must stop and remain stopped until the lights are turned off.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 29, PA p. 62, CA p. 57)

prompt: On a two-lane road, a school bus coming toward you stops with its red lights flashing. What must you do?
choices: Keep going, because the bus is not in your lane
Slow down and pass carefully
Stop, even though the bus is on the other side of the road
Stop only if children are crossing in front of you
explanation: On a two-lane road, traffic in both directions must stop for a school bus with flashing red lights. Children may cross the road in front of you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 57, TX p. 29, NY p. 40)

prompt: A school bus is stopped with its red lights flashing, but you do not see any children. What should you do?
choices: Pass slowly, since no children are present
Honk and then pass
Stop briefly, then go around the bus
Stop anyway and wait until the red lights stop flashing
explanation: You must stop for flashing red lights whether or not you see children. Children can be hidden by the bus or may be about to cross.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 29, PA p. 62, NY p. 68)

prompt: After waiting for a stopped school bus, its red lights turn off and it starts to move. What should you do?
choices: Look for children near the road and drive slowly until you are past them
Speed up to get ahead of the bus
Pass the bus right away on the right
Honk to let children know you are going
explanation: Children may still be near the bus or along the road after it leaves. Watch for them and drive slowly until you have passed them.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 40, PA p. 62)

prompt: When are children around a school bus in the most danger?
choices: While they are seated on a moving bus
When the bus is parked at the school
When the bus is on the highway
When they cross the street after getting off the bus
explanation: Most school bus-related deaths and injuries happen to children crossing the street after leaving the bus, not in bus crashes. That is why traffic must stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 40)

prompt: What should you do at a railroad crossing marked only with a crossbuck (white X-shaped) sign?
choices: Stop every time, even if no train is coming
Keep your speed, because there are no lights or gates
Treat it like a yield sign: slow down, look, listen, and stop if a train is coming
Speed up to cross the tracks quickly
explanation: A crossbuck means you must yield to trains. Slow down, look both ways, listen, and be ready to stop if a train is approaching.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 14, FL p. 64, TX p. 28)

prompt: Why must drivers always yield to trains at crossings?
choices: Trains cannot stop quickly or steer to avoid you
Trains always travel at very low speeds
Train engineers can see far enough ahead to stop
Trains sound their horns, so they can wait for you
explanation: A train can take a mile or more to stop and cannot swerve. Trains always have the right-of-way at crossings.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 155, TX p. 28, CA p. 58)

prompt: Traffic is backed up on the other side of a railroad crossing, and there is not enough room for your car past the tracks. What should you do?
choices: Drive onto the tracks and wait there
Wait before the tracks until there is room to cross completely
Follow the car ahead closely so you are not left behind
Cross and stop partly on the tracks
explanation: Never stop on railroad tracks. Do not start across until there is room for your whole vehicle on the other side.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 58, NJ p. 155, PA p. 59)

prompt: You are stopped at a crossing with two sets of tracks. A train has just passed. What should you do before crossing?
choices: Go as soon as the last car of the train passes
Go as soon as the gates start to rise
Follow the car in front of you
Wait until you can clearly see that no other train is coming on any track
explanation: One train can hide another coming on a different track. Wait until you have a clear view in both directions on all tracks.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 59, TX p. 28, CA p. 57)

prompt: The gates at a railroad crossing are down, but you do not see a train. What should you do?
choices: Drive around the gates slowly
Drive around if no train is visible in either direction
Stay stopped; never drive around the gates
Back up and cross on the other side of the gate
explanation: Never go around or under lowered gates. If they stay down and no train comes, call the number on the posted emergency sign or 911.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 57, FL p. 64, TX p. 28)

prompt: Your car stalls on the railroad tracks and a train is coming. What should you do?
choices: Stay in the car and keep trying to start it
Get everyone out at once and move away from the tracks at an angle toward the approaching train
Run away along the tracks in the same direction the train is going
Get out and stand next to the car to wave down the train
explanation: Leave the vehicle immediately. Moving away at an angle toward the train helps you avoid being hit by your car or flying debris after the crash.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 76, NJ p. 155, FL p. 88)

prompt: Your car stalls on railroad tracks and no train is in sight. After getting everyone out, who should you call first?
choices: Your insurance company
A tow truck company
The local department of motor vehicles
The phone number on the blue emergency sign posted at the crossing
explanation: The blue Emergency Notification System sign gives the railroad's emergency number and a crossing ID. Calling it can get trains stopped; then call 911.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 76, TX p. 28, FL p. 88)

prompt: Why do drivers often misjudge how close a train is?
choices: A train's large size makes it look farther away and slower than it really is
Trains always travel slower than cars
Trains are lit only at night
Trains slow down when they near a crossing
explanation: A train is usually closer and moving faster than it appears. Never try to race a train to a crossing.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 155)

prompt: Why should you stop well back from the tracks when a train is coming?
choices: The ground near the tracks is too soft
Trains are wider than the rails, so they can hit a car stopped too close
So the engineer can read your license plate
Because trains can switch to a different track at the crossing
explanation: A train hangs out several feet beyond the rails on each side. Stop behind the stop line or gate, never right next to the tracks.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 155)

prompt: You cross the same railroad tracks every day and have never seen a train there. How should you treat the crossing?
choices: Cross without slowing, since trains do not use those tracks
Look only during the morning rush hour
Look only if the warning lights are flashing
Look and listen every time, because a train can come at any time from either direction
explanation: Familiar crossings can be the most dangerous because drivers stop expecting trains. Expect a train on any track, at any time, in either direction.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 59, CA p. 58, NJ p. 155)

prompt: The car ahead of you crosses the railroad tracks without stopping. What should you do?
choices: Follow it closely, since the driver must have checked for trains
Speed up to cross before the gates come down
Check for trains yourself and make sure there is room past the tracks before you go
Pass it before the crossing so you are not delayed
explanation: Do not blindly follow another vehicle across tracks. Look and listen for yourself, and never try to pass another vehicle near a crossing.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 59)

prompt: On a two-way street, an ambulance with its siren on and lights flashing comes up behind you. What should you do?
choices: Speed up to stay ahead of it
Pull to the right edge of the road and stop until it passes
Stop right where you are in your lane
Pull to the left so it can pass on the right
explanation: Yield to emergency vehicles using a siren and flashing lights by pulling to the right edge of the road and stopping until they have passed.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 51, TX p. 28, PA p. 63)

prompt: You are in the middle of an intersection when you hear a siren coming toward you. What should you do?
choices: Stop right away in the intersection
Continue through the intersection, then pull to the right and stop
Back up out of the intersection
Turn left to get out of the way
explanation: Do not stop inside an intersection. Clear it first, then pull over to the right as soon as it is safe and stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 51, FL p. 92, PA p. 63)

prompt: A fire truck with its siren on has just passed you. What should you do before pulling back into traffic?
choices: Check that no other emergency vehicles are coming
Pull out right away and follow the fire truck
Honk to let others know you are pulling out
Wait until you can no longer hear the siren
explanation: Emergency vehicles often travel in groups. Look and listen for more of them before you return to the road.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 63)

prompt: Traffic is heavy, and a police car with siren and lights just went by. Is it a good idea to follow closely behind it to get through traffic?
choices: Yes, if you keep your hazard lights on
Yes, because it is clearing the road for you
Yes, as long as you stay in the same lane
No, you must stay well back from an emergency vehicle that is answering a call
explanation: Following closely behind an emergency vehicle that is using its siren or lights is dangerous and not allowed. How far back you must stay depends on your state.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 51, TX p. 28, PA p. 63)

prompt: An ambulance with its siren on is behind you, but parked cars line the right side and there is no room to pull over. What should you do?
choices: Stop right where you are, even if you block the lane
Slow down and leave a clear path for the ambulance, pulling over when you can
Speed up to find a better place, even above the speed limit
Move into the oncoming lane
explanation: If you cannot pull to the right, slow down and keep a clear path for the emergency vehicle, then pull over as soon as it is safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 28, CA p. 51)

prompt: What does an orange triangle with a red border on the back of a vehicle mean?
choices: It is a slow-moving vehicle, so slow down
It is carrying hazardous materials
It is an emergency vehicle
It is a wide load that must be passed on the right
explanation: The orange and red triangle marks vehicles that travel much slower than normal traffic, such as farm equipment, horse-drawn vehicles and road machinery.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 51, NY p. 76, AZ p. 52, TX p. 43)

prompt: A wide farm tractor ahead of you on a two-lane road moves toward the left. What might the driver be doing?
choices: Pulling over to let you pass on the right
Getting ready to stop on the left shoulder
Swinging wide to make a right turn, so do not try to pass yet
Signaling you to pass on the right
explanation: Farm equipment may swing left before turning right and may not have turn signals. Hang back until you know what the driver is doing.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 52)

prompt: You are stuck behind slow farm equipment on a two-lane road. What should you do?
choices: Pass right away, even on a curve, since it is so slow
Be patient and pass only where it is legal and you can see that it is safe
Follow closely so the driver knows to pull over
Honk until the driver moves onto the shoulder
explanation: Slow-moving vehicles have the right to use the road. Stay back where you can see, and pass only when it is legal and safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 52, NY p. 76, PA p. 48)

prompt: On a rural highway, why is it important to spot a slow-moving vehicle as early as possible?
choices: So you can speed up and pass before oncoming traffic arrives
Because slow-moving vehicles must pull over when they see you
You close in on it very quickly, and seeing it early gives you time to slow down safely
It is not important, since slow vehicles stay on the shoulder
explanation: At highway speed you approach a slow vehicle fast. Spotting it early gives you time to slow down or change lanes; braking suddenly can cause a crash.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., MT p. 72, CA p. 51)

prompt: You come up behind a person riding a horse along the road. What should you do?
choices: Honk so the rider knows you are passing
Pass quickly so the horse is not near traffic long
Slow down, give plenty of room, and do not honk
Rev your engine to warn the rider
explanation: Loud noises and fast passing can scare a horse. Slow down, pass wide, and avoid using your horn.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 76, PA p. 63, CA p. 52)

prompt: You stop behind a horse-drawn vehicle at a stop sign. Why should you leave plenty of room?
choices: So the horse can turn around
Horse-drawn vehicles can roll backward after stopping
It is required only if the horse is unhitched
So you can pass it on the right
explanation: After stopping, a horse-drawn vehicle may roll back. Following too closely also keeps the driver from seeing you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 63)

prompt: You have just passed a horse-drawn vehicle. When should you move back into the right lane?
choices: Only after leaving plenty of space between your car and the horse
As soon as your car is beside the horse
Right away, then tap your brakes to warn the driver
As soon as the horse's driver waves
explanation: Pulling back in too soon can spook the horse. Leave enough space before you return to the lane.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 63)

prompt: You see cattle near the edge of a rural road. What should you do?
choices: Slow down or stop, and go on only when it is safe
Honk to scare them away from the road
Speed up to get past before they move
Flash your high beams and keep your speed
explanation: When animals or livestock are near the road, slow down or stop and proceed carefully. Follow directions from anyone in charge of the animals.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 52, NJ p. 157)

prompt: A deer runs across the road in front of you and disappears into the trees. What should you expect?
choices: The danger is over once it has crossed
More deer may follow, so slow down and watch carefully
The deer will come back across right away
Deer always travel alone
explanation: Deer and similar animals often travel in groups. If you see one, look for more.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., MT p. 71, NE p. 34, AK p. 72)

prompt: A deer suddenly steps onto the road too close to stop in time. Oncoming traffic is in the other lane. What is the safest action?
choices: Swerve sharply into the oncoming lane
Brake firmly and stay in your lane
Swerve off the road onto the shoulder at full speed
Speed up to get past the deer
explanation: Swerving can send you into oncoming traffic or off the road, which is often worse than hitting the animal. Brake firmly, steer to keep control, and stop safely.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NE p. 34, MT p. 71, NJ p. 157)

prompt: A flagger in a work zone holds up a sign showing STOP. What should you do?
choices: Stop and wait until the flagger signals you to go
Slow down and drive past carefully
Stop briefly, then go if the road looks clear
Follow the car in front of you
explanation: Flaggers use STOP/SLOW paddles or red flags to control traffic. Stop and wait until the flagger lets you proceed.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 44, AR p. 34, CA p. 55)

prompt: In a work zone, the flagger's signals conflict with a nearby traffic light. Which should you obey?
choices: The traffic light
Whichever lets you go sooner
The flagger
Whichever signal you saw first
explanation: Directions from flaggers and police officers take priority over normal signs and signals in a work zone.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AR p. 34, CA p. 55, CA p. 51)

prompt: A flagger in a work zone turns the paddle to show SLOW. What does this mean?
choices: Stop and wait for another signal
Pull onto the shoulder
Proceed slowly and with caution
Speed up to clear the work area
explanation: The SLOW side of a flagger's paddle means you may move ahead carefully at a reduced speed, watching for workers.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 44, AR p. 34)
